title: Technical MCQ Set 05: Async Java, Unix Inodes & MVCC
description: Tests CompletableFuture, WeakHashMap, Unix inode capacity numericals, MVCC, UNION vs UNION ALL, Trie complexity, and HTTP/2.

questions.question: What does the following Java regex snippet print?
questions.explanation: `.*?` is a reluctant (non-greedy) quantifier, so it stops at the FIRST closing ``, matching `one`. A greedy `.*` would match across the entire string to the final ``.

questions.question: What does this Java class print when `main` executes?
questions.explanation: Java forbids referencing a static field by simple name before its textual declaration in an initializer (`a = b + 1` before `b` is declared), causing a compile-time `illegal forward reference` error (unless accessed via `InitOrder.b`).

questions.question: Which statement describes the behavior of the following Java inheritance code?
options: Compilation error: return type `Dog` is incompatible with `Animal`
Compiles cleanly because `Dog` is a covariant return type (subtype of `Animal`)
questions.explanation: Since Java 5, an overriding method may return a subtype (covariant return type) of the superclass method's reference return type.

questions.question: You have `CompletableFuture<User> fetchUser(id)` and `CompletableFuture<List<Order>> fetchOrders(User u)`. Which method chains them into a flat `CompletableFuture<List<Order>>`?
questions.explanation: `thenApply` would wrap the result into nested `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<List<Order>>>`, whereas `thenCompose` flattens dependent asynchronous stages (like `flatMap`).

questions.question: How does `WeakHashMap<K, V>` differ from `HashMap<K, V>` regarding garbage collection?
options: Values are wrapped in weak references while keys stay strong
Entries are automatically eligible for eviction once their key has no other strong references anywhere in the JVM
It prevents garbage collection from ever running on keys
It stores all entries off-heap in native memory
questions.explanation: `WeakHashMap` wraps each key in a `WeakReference`. Once the application drops all strong references to a key, GC reclaims the key and `WeakHashMap` clears the stale entry via its `ReferenceQueue`.

questions.question: If class `Invoice` implements `Cloneable`, calls `super.clone()`, and holds a mutable `List<LineItem> items`, what happens when a caller mutates `clonedInvoice.items.add(...)`?
options: Both the original `Invoice` and `clonedInvoice` see the added item because `super.clone()` copies only the `items` reference (shallow copy)
Java automatically performs a deep copy of all `Collection` fields
questions.explanation: `Object.clone()` performs a field-by-field shallow copy; mutable reference fields point to the exact same heap object unless explicitly deep-copied inside `clone()`.

questions.question: Why is `UNION ALL` typically significantly faster than `UNION` when combining two large query results that are already known to be disjoint?
options: `UNION ALL` appends rows directly without performing an expensive sort/hash deduplication pass to eliminate duplicates
`UNION ALL` runs only on read replicas
questions.explanation: `UNION` removes duplicate rows across the combined set (requiring sorting or hashing), whereas `UNION ALL` streams all rows straight through in O(N) without deduplication.

questions.subtopic: GROUP BY with HAVING Aggregate Filter
questions.question: Which query correctly finds departments whose average salary exceeds 70,000, considering only employees hired after 2022?
options: `SELECT dept_id FROM Emp WHERE AVG(salary) > 70000 AND hire_year > 2022 GROUP BY dept_id`
`SELECT dept_id FROM Emp WHERE hire_year > 2022 GROUP BY dept_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 70000`
`SELECT dept_id FROM Emp GROUP BY dept_id HAVING hire_year > 2022 AND AVG(salary) > 70000`
`SELECT dept_id FROM Emp HAVING AVG(salary) > 70000 WHERE hire_year > 2022`
questions.explanation: Row-level conditions (`hire_year > 2022`) belong in `WHERE` before grouping; aggregate conditions (`AVG(salary) > 70000`) belong in `HAVING` after `GROUP BY`.

questions.question: A table `Enrollment(student_id, course_id, grade, course_title)` has primary key `(student_id, course_id)`, and `course_id -> course_title`. Which normal form is violated?
options: 2NF (partial functional dependency on part of a composite key)
questions.explanation: Non-prime attribute `course_title` depends on only a proper subset (`course_id`) of the composite candidate key `(student_id, course_id)`—a partial dependency violating 2NF.

questions.question: How does Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) in PostgreSQL allow `SELECT` queries to run concurrently with `UPDATE` transactions without blocking each other?
options: By locking the entire database file for 10 ms slices
By keeping older row tuple versions tagged with transaction IDs so readers view a consistent snapshot without acquiring read locks
By disabling ACID isolation for all `SELECT` queries
By duplicating the whole table in RAM on every `SELECT`
questions.explanation: MVCC retains prior tuple versions so writers never block readers and readers never block writers; each transaction sees row versions valid as of its snapshot transaction ID.

questions.question: A Unix-like filesystem uses 4 KB disk blocks and 4-byte block pointers. An inode has 10 direct pointers, 1 single-indirect pointer, and 1 double-indirect pointer. Approximately what is the maximum file size supported?
questions.explanation: Pointers per block = 4096 / 4 = 1024. Direct = 10 * 4 KB = 40 KB. Single indirect = 1024 * 4 KB = 4 MB. Double indirect = 1024 * 1024 * 4 KB = 4,194,304 KB = 4 GB. Total ≈ 4 GB + 4 MB + 40 KB (~4 GB).

questions.question: Which distinction between Deadlock and Starvation is accurate?
options: In deadlock, processes are blocked permanently waiting for each other; in starvation, a runnable process is perpetually denied CPU/resources due to scheduling bias (e.g., strict priority)
Starvation can only occur on single-core CPUs, while deadlock requires 4+ cores
Deadlock is solved by aging, whereas starvation requires killing all OS threads
They are identical terms for memory leaks
questions.explanation: Deadlocked processes cannot progress under any schedule without intervention (mutual circular wait), whereas a starving process is ready to run but continuously bypassed (fixed via priority aging).

questions.question: In the classic Dining Philosophers problem with 5 philosophers, making Philosophers 0–3 pick up their LEFT fork first while Philosopher 4 picks up their RIGHT fork first prevents deadlock because it breaks:
questions.explanation: Reversing fork acquisition order for one philosopher assigns a global fork hierarchy, making a circular wait cycle impossible.

questions.question: How does HTTP/2 eliminate application-layer HTTP Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking compared to HTTP/1.1 pipelining?
options: By running over UDP instead of TCP
By multiplexing independent bidirectional binary streams (frames) concurrently over a single TCP connection
By disabling TLS encryption on static assets
By opening 100 separate TCP connections per webpage
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 splits requests/responses into tagged binary frames across concurrent streams over one TCP connection, so one slow response no longer stalls other HTTP responses (though TCP packet-loss HoL still remains until HTTP/3 QUIC).

questions.question: With a 30 ms round-trip time (RTT) between client and server (ignoring TLS and transmission time), how long after the client sends `SYN` does the client receive the first HTTP response byte if the HTTP `GET` is sent immediately after the 3-way handshake?
questions.explanation: 1 RTT (30 ms) for `SYN` -> `SYN-ACK`; client then sends `ACK` pipelined with HTTP `GET`, and receives the first HTTP response byte 1 RTT later => 2 * 30 = 60 ms.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity to search for a string of length `L` inside a Trie storing `N` dictionary words over a constant alphabet size (e.g., 26 lowercase letters)?
questions.explanation: A Trie walks at most `L` characters down from the root using O(1) array indexing per character, independent of the total number of stored words `N`.

questions.question: In standard non-empty Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's algorithm), if an array contains ALL negative numbers (e.g., `[-8, -3, -6, -2, -5]`), what must the algorithm return?
questions.explanation: If initialized properly (`cur = arr[0]`, `best = arr[0]`, updating `cur = max(arr[i], cur + arr[i])`), Kadane's handles all-negative arrays and returns the largest single element `-2` rather than erroneously clamping to `0`.

questions.question: Which JDBC interface is specifically designed to invoke database stored procedures with `IN`, `OUT`, and `INOUT` parameters?
questions.explanation: `CallableStatement` (created via `conn.prepareCall("{call proc_name(?, ?)}")`) supports `registerOutParameter()` for stored procedure `OUT`/`INOUT` values.

questions.question: In Spring MVC / Spring Boot, `@RestController` is a convenience stereotype annotation combining which two annotations?
questions.explanation: `@RestController` combines `@Controller` and `@ResponseBody`, instructing Spring to serialize return values directly to the HTTP response body (e.g., JSON via Jackson) instead of resolving HTML view names.

questions.question: In Scrum, what does a Sprint Burndown Chart plot over the days of a sprint?
options: Total lines of code committed per developer
Remaining estimated work (story points or hours) vs days remaining in the sprint
Cumulative production uptime across AWS regions
questions.explanation: A Sprint Burndown Chart tracks remaining sprint backlog effort (y-axis) across sprint days (x-axis) against an ideal diagonal pace line.

questions.question: What does `System.out.println(10 + 20 + "HCL" + 10 + 20);` output?
questions.explanation: `+` is left-associative: `10 + 20` performs integer addition (`30`), then `30 + "HCL"` yields String `"30HCL"`, after which `+ 10` and `+ 20` perform String concatenation => `30HCL1020`.

questions.question: Where must `ORDER BY` be placed when sorting the combined output of two `SELECT` statements joined by `UNION`?
options: At the end of the FIRST `SELECT` only
Once at the very end of the LAST `SELECT`, referencing column names/aliases from the first `SELECT`
questions.explanation: Standard SQL permits a single final `ORDER BY` after the last query in a `UNION` to sort the combined result set (column aliases come from the first `SELECT`).

questions.subtopic: Space Complexity of Merge Sort vs Quick Sort
questions.question: Comparing standard array-based Merge Sort and in-place Quick Sort on `N` elements, what is their auxiliary space complexity?
options: Merge Sort: `O(N)` auxiliary buffer, Quick Sort: `O(log N)` average recursion stack (`O(N)` worst-case)
Both always use `O(N log N)` auxiliary space
questions.explanation: Standard Merge Sort allocates an `O(N)` temporary array for merging, whereas in-place Quick Sort requires only `O(log N)` call-stack space on balanced partitions (`O(N)` worst-case).

questions.question: When is a Spinlock preferable to a sleeping/blocking Mutex?
options: On a single-core CPU for holding a lock during slow disk I/O
On a multi-core CPU when the lock is held for an extremely short duration (shorter than two context switches)
Whenever threads want to yield CPU time to background applications
In Java Swing UI event-dispatch threads waiting for user clicks
questions.explanation: Spinlocks busy-wait without triggering an OS context switch; on multi-core systems for tiny critical sections (nanoseconds), spinning is cheaper than sleeping + waking a thread, whereas on a single core spinning wastes the entire time slice.

questions.question: Which protocol is used for SENDING/relaying outbound email between mail servers, and which is used for multi-device synchronized folder retrieval?
options: IMAP for sending; SMTP for retrieval
SMTP for sending/relaying; IMAP for synchronized server-side folder retrieval
POP3 for sending; DNS MX for folder sync
HTTP POST for server-to-server relay; SNMP for retrieval
questions.explanation: SMTP pushes/relays outbound mail between clients and mail servers, while IMAP keeps mail and folder state synchronized on the server across multiple client devices.
